claim: Associative learning, but not passive odor exposure, potentiates the strength of sensory inputs up to several weeks after the end of training in adult mice.
source: Here we show that associative learning, but not passive odor exposure, potentiates the strength of sensory inputs up to several weeks after the end of training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral training and imaging experiments presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Experience-dependent plasticity can occur in the periphery of adult mouse olfactory system.
source: We conclude that experience-dependent plasticity can occur in the periphery of adult mouse olfactory system, which should improve odor detection and contribute towards accurate and fast odor discriminations.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing changes in sensory input strength following olfactory learning.

claim: Both structural and functional plasticity have been reported in different sensory systems during development and in adulthood following lesions, passive experience or learning.
source: Both structural and functional plasticity have been reported in different sensory systems during development and in adulthood following lesions, passive experience or learning (Recanzone et al., 1993; Bao et al., 2001; Polley et al., 2004; Accolla and Carleton, 2008; Keck et al., 2008; Hofer et al., 2009; Carleton et al., 2010; Rosselet et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Attention has been mostly focused on plasticity mechanisms in higher brain areas, mainly in the cortex.
source: While attention has been mostly focused on plasticity mechanisms in higher brain areas (i.e., mainly in the cortex) (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Bao et al., 2001; Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Accolla and Carleton, 2008; Carleton et al., 2010; Rosselet et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2012), less is known about the functional changes at earlier stages of sensory processing, especially in response to sensory learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a characterization of the field.

claim: Less is known about the functional changes at earlier stages of sensory processing, especially in response to sensory learning.
source: While attention has been mostly focused on plasticity mechanisms in higher brain areas (i.e., mainly in the cortex) (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Bao et al., 2001; Feldman and Brecht, 2005; Accolla and Carleton, 2008; Carleton et al., 2010; Rosselet et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2012), less is known about the functional changes at earlier stages of sensory processing, especially in response to sensory learning.
evidence: This claim characterizes a gap in scientific knowledge based on the literature.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons expressing one specialized odorant receptor gene converge in a receptor-specific manner onto glomeruli in the main olfactory bulb.
source: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) expressing one specialized odorant receptor gene out of a large repertoire (Malnic et al., 1999) converge in a receptor-specific manner onto anatomical structures in the main olfactory bulb (OB) called glomeruli (Ressler et al., 1994; Mombaerts et al., 1996; Sakano, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established research in the field.

claim: Odorants activate complex spatio-temporal patterns of glomeruli.
source: Odorants activate complex spatio-temporal patterns of glomeruli, which can be monitored with various imaging techniques (Rubin and Katz, 1999; Uchida et al., 2000; Wachowiak and Cohen, 2001; Spors and Grinvald, 2002; Bozza et al., 2004; Bathellier et al., 2007; Vincis et al., 2012; Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous imaging studies.

claim: Several plasticity mechanisms have been reported in olfactory cortical regions.
source: Several plasticity mechanisms have been reported in olfactory cortical regions (Quinlan et al., 2004; Franks and Isaacson, 2005; Stripling and Galupo, 2008) as well as OB circuitry (Saghatelyan et al., 2005; Marks et al., 2006; Gao and Strowbridge, 2009; Livneh and Mizrahi, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both sensory deprivation and developmental reorganization have been reported to induce structural plasticity in the glomerular layer.
source: At the input level, both sensory deprivation (Cummings et al., 1997) and developmental reorganization (Zou et al., 2004; Kerr and Belluscio, 2006) have been reported to induce structural plasticity in the glomerular layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Little is known about learning-mediated functional plasticity of sensory inputs in the adult OB of awake mice.
source: Despite these facts, little is known about learning-mediated functional plasticity of sensory inputs in the adult OB of awake mice.
evidence: This claim characterizes a gap in scientific knowledge.

claim: Performance levels reached more than 80% of correct responses after 400 trials for Cin vs Eu discrimination at 100 dilution.
source: Performance levels reached more than 80% of correct responses after 400 trials and remained high during the following sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Performance levels remained close to chance levels for 10−10 and 10−5 dilutions of Cin vs Eu, which can be interpreted as a lack of perception/discrimination.
source: The performance levels remained close to chance levels for 10−10 and 10−5 dilutions, which can be interpreted as a lack of perception/discrimination (Figure 2A, no difference between the two dilutions, Fisher's Least Significant Difference [LSD] test, p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: Mice started to discriminate Cin vs Eu from 10−3 onwards on average.
source: On average, mice started to discriminate from 10−3 onwards (note that one mouse was able to discriminate at 10−5 with an accuracy of ∼70%, Figure 2B), reaching ∼70% of correct responses for 10−3 dilution and >90% for 10−2, 10−1 and 100 dilutions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Performance levels remained close to chance levels for 10−10 and 10−8 dilutions of IAA vs EB.
source: Performance levels remained close to chance levels for 10−10 and 10−8 dilutions (no difference between the two dilutions, LSD, p>0.1, paired comparison), but mice showed a tendency to learn at 10−6 dilution and hence were trained at this dilution for an additional 300 trials during which their performance reached 80% of correct responses (comparison between first and second task of 300 trials 10−6 IAA/EB, LSD test p<0.005).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: For lower dilutions (10−4, 10−2 and 100) of IAA vs EB, mice performed systematically above 90%.
source: For lower dilutions (10−4, 10−2 and 100), mice performed systematically above 90% (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Reaction times decreased with the odorant dilution, reflecting a direct linear correlation with performance levels.
source: Across all concentrations, reaction times decreased with the odorant dilution, reflecting a direct linear correlation with performance levels (R2 = 0.74, ANOVA F = 12.3 p=0.04 and R2 = 0.82, ANOVA F = 23.2 p=0.0085 for Cin/Eu and IAA/EB tasks, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: Mice discriminated the dilutions 10−2, 10−1 and 100 of Cin vs Eu with similar reaction times.
source: Mice discriminated the dilutions 10−2, 10−1 and 100 of Cin vs Eu with similar reaction times (Figure 2D, one-way repeated measures ANOVA, F = 2.84, p=0.13).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis.

claim: The discrimination thresholds for Cin/Eu and IAA/EB are between 10−5 and 10−3 and between 10−8 and 10−6, respectively.
source: For the population of trained animals, we therefore estimate that the discrimination thresholds for Cin/Eu and IAA/EB are between 10−5 and 10−3 and between 10−8 and 10−6, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral data analysis.

claim: For odorant dilutions lower than the discrimination threshold, no activated glomeruli could be detected on the dorsal OB of any group of mice.
source: For odorant dilutions lower than the discrimination threshold (≤10−5 and 10−8 for Cin/Eu and EB/IAA, respectively), we could not detect any activated glomeruli on the dorsal OB of any group of mice (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: For odorant dilutions above the discrimination threshold, more activated glomeruli were observed in trained animals than in naïve or exposed mice.
source: For odorant dilutions above the discrimination threshold (10−3 to 10−2 and 10−6 to 10−4 for Cin/Eu and EB/IAA, respectively; referred as high dilution hereafter), we observed more activated glomeruli in trained animals than in naïve or exposed mice, an effect consistent across all odorants used for training (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A threefold increase in the average number of activated glomeruli was observed among trained mice.
source: On average we observed a threefold increase in the average number of activated glomeruli among the trained mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The enhancement in number of activated glomeruli was due to associative learning and not due to simple exposure to the odorants.
source: This enhancement was due to the associative learning and not due to simple exposure to the odorants since the animals passively exposed to the same stimuli and for the same amount of time did not show a significant change in the number of glomeruli in comparison to naïve mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of imaging data across experimental groups.

claim: At lower dilutions, the number of activated glomeruli remained similar across the three groups (trained, naïve, exposed).
source: At lower dilutions (10−1 to 100 and 10−2 to 100 for Cin/Eu and EB/IAA, respectively; referred as low dilution hereafter) the number of activated glomeruli remained similar across the three groups (Figure 3F), suggesting that associative learning indeed improves the sensitivity of sensory inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: Associative learning improves the sensitivity of sensory inputs.
source: At lower dilutions (10−1 to 100 and 10−2 to 100 for Cin/Eu and EB/IAA, respectively; referred as low dilution hereafter) the number of activated glomeruli remained similar across the three groups (Figure 3F), suggesting that associative learning indeed improves the sensitivity of sensory inputs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that more glomeruli are activated at higher dilutions in trained mice.

claim: The amplitude of the evoked activity did not differ among the passively exposed and naïve group of mice.
source: The amplitude of the evoked activity did not differ among the passively exposed and naïve group of mice (Figure 4A–D, LSD test p=0.7, 0.23, 0.81 and 0.2 for IAA, EB, Cin and Eu).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Trained mice consistently showed enhanced IOS amplitudes compared to control groups.
source: In contrast, compared to these control groups, trained mice consistently showed enhanced IOS amplitudes (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: A form of functional plasticity is induced in OB sensory inputs by olfactory learning, but not by passive exposure to the same odorants.
source: In summary, a form of functional plasticity is induced in OB sensory inputs by an olfactory learning, but not by a passive exposure to the same odorants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of imaging data across experimental groups.

claim: The potentiation induced by learning was independent of the chemical class and the dilution of the stimuli.
source: This potentiation was independent of the chemical class and the dilution of the stimuli (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The amplitude of the glomerular responses evoked across all dilutions was not significantly different between the rewarded and non-rewarded stimuli.
source: However the amplitude of the glomerular responses evoked across all dilutions was not significantly different between the rewarded and non-rewarded stimuli (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: The learning-induced potentiation is visible for all dilutions and lasts up to 5 weeks.
source: We compared the amplitude of the evoked glomerular responses across the three groups and found that the learning-induced potentiation is visible for all dilutions and lasts up to 5 weeks (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data collected at different time points after training.

claim: Olfactory learning induces a form of functional plasticity at the sensory input level, which is long lasting and independent of the stimulus reward value.
source: In conclusion, olfactory learning induces a form of functional plasticity at the sensory input level, which is long lasting and independent of the stimulus reward value.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing potentiation lasting weeks and similar effects for rewarded and non-rewarded stimuli.

claim: Olfactory learning induces the potentiation of sensory inputs to the OB, increasing both the number of activated glomeruli and the strength of activation when compared to control animals.
source: Olfactory learning induces the potentiation of sensory inputs to the OB, increasing both the number of activated glomeruli and the strength of activation when compared to control animals.
evidence: This claim summarizes the imaging data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The relationship between discrimination performance levels and measured glomerular response amplitudes for different odorant dilutions was well fitted with a Boltzmann function for both discrimination tasks.
source: These data were well fitted with a Boltzmann function for both discrimination tasks (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and curve fitting shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the rising phase of the curves, corresponding to the dilutions around discrimination threshold, a small change in input strength caused strong improvement in discrimination accuracy.
source: In the rising phase of the curves, corresponding to the dilutions around discrimination threshold, a small change in input strength caused strong improvement in discrimination accuracy.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of the relationship between input strength and performance shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At dilutions close to discrimination threshold, an increase in the performance level correlated with an increase in input strength.
source: At these specific dilutions, an increase in the performance level (Figure 5B) correlated with an increase in input strength; either by an increase in the number of activated glomeruli or by an increase in the amplitude of glomerular responses (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation analysis presented in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The trained animals would be able to detect and eventually discriminate more easily and rapidly odorants at lower concentrations than control animals.
source: Since we observed that the learning process potentiated the inputs to the olfactory bulb, we propose that the trained animals would be able to detect and eventually discriminate more easily and rapidly odorants at lower concentrations than control animals (i.e., naïve and exposed groups).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the observed potentiation of inputs.

claim: The discrimination threshold for odorants could potentially be shifted by few orders of concentration magnitude.
source: The discrimination threshold for odorants could potentially be shifted by few orders of concentration magnitude.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed effects of training.

claim: The reported form of functional plasticity differs from previously reported plastic changes observed during the postnatal maturation of the olfactory system.
source: The reported form of functional plasticity, induced by sensory experience, in the glomerular layer of the adult mouse olfactory system differs from previously reported plastic changes observed during the postnatal maturation of the olfactory system (Zou et al., 2004; Kerr and Belluscio, 2006).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous research cited.

claim: During the first 2 months of postnatal life, a refinement of OSN projections occurs, leading to a glomerulus receiving only afferents from sensory neurons expressing the same receptor.
source: During the first 2 months of postnatal life (Zou et al., 2004), a refinement of the projections occurs, leading to the known concept of a glomerulus receiving only afferents from sensory neurons expressing the same receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: This form of structural plasticity during development is accelerated by sensory experience.
source: This form of structural plasticity is accelerated by sensory experience (Kerr and Belluscio, 2006), but it is not known if this causes any change in sensory input strength.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The observed plasticity in this study is induced during adulthood outside the developmental window and is associated with the increase of input strength.
source: In our study, the observed plasticity is induced during adulthood outside this developmental window, when one glomerulus is homogeneously innervated by one type of sensory neurons, and is associated to the increase of input strength.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current findings from developmental plasticity.

claim: Associative learning causes a form of plasticity whereas a passive repetitive exposure did not.
source: All forms of sensory experience are not equivalent in triggering plasticity of the sensory inputs. Indeed, we report that associative learning causes a form of plasticity whereas a passive repetitive exposure did not, as similarly observed in cortical areas of other sensory systems (Bao et al., 2001; Accolla and Carleton, 2008; Rosselet et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and comparison with previous research.

claim: The passively exposed group of mice did not show any change in the input strength compared to the naïve ones.
source: The passively exposed group of mice did not show any change in the input strength compared to the naïve ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by the imaging data comparing exposed and naïve groups.

claim: The lack of effect during passive exposure is consistent with a recent study.
source: Though we cannot rule out this possibility, the lack of effect during passive exposure is consistent with a recent study (Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Long passive exposure (16 hr daily during 2–6 weeks) has been reported to enhance input sensitivity.
source: On the other hand, it is contrasting with the previously reported enhancement of input sensitivity following long passive exposure (Wang et al., 1993). In our study the total exposure time was less than an hour for one class of chemical stimuli (including all dilutions) whereas the exposure time was much longer in the latter study (16 hr daily during 2–6 weeks).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The associative learning paradigm potentiated the input strength for several odorants independently of their chemical class and reward value.
source: Our associative learning paradigm potentiated the input strength for several odorants independently of their chemical class and reward value.
evidence: This claim is supported by the imaging data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Previous reports showed that training specifically affected the odorant representation of the rewarded stimulus or the stimulus associated with a foot shock.
source: Previous reports showed that training specifically affected the odorant representation of the rewarded stimulus (Faber et al., 1999) or the stimulus associated with a foot shock (Kass et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The enhancement of sensory input strength for both odorants could activate the inhibitory neurons of the olfactory bulb thereby helping the refinement and the discrimination between odorants.
source: The enhancement of sensory input strength for both odorants could activate the inhibitory neurons of the olfactory bulb thereby helping the refinement and the discrimination between odorants (Abraham et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the behavioral relevance of the findings.

claim: IOS imaging is primarily monitoring neurotransmitter release from OSNs as evidenced by pharmacology experiments.
source: IOS imaging is primarily monitoring neurotransmitter release from OSNs as evidenced by pharmacology experiments (Gurden et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Studies comparing IOS with presynaptic-specific imaging readouts provide additional evidence supporting the presynaptic origin of IOS signals in the OB.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out a possible postsynaptic contribution to the signal, studies comparing IOS with presynaptic-specific imaging readouts provide additional evidence supporting the presynaptic origin of IOS signals in the OB (Wachowiak and Cohen, 2003; Soucy et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A similar potentiation of the odor-evoked glomeruli activity induced by fear learning has been recently reported in anesthetized animals while monitoring a genetically encoded reporter of activity expressed specifically in OSNs.
source: In addition, a similar potentiation of the odor-evoked glomeruli activity induced by fear learning has been recently reported in anesthetized animals while monitoring a genetically encoded reporter of activity expressed specifically in OSNs (Kass et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The plasticity is associated with change in OSN activity.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the plasticity is associated with change in OSN activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the IOS imaging data and comparison with other studies.

claim: OSN sensitivity could be enhanced, leading to an increase of the odor evoked OSN firing rate causing more release of glutamate in the glomerulus.
source: Firstly, OSN sensitivity could be enhanced, leading to an increase of the odor evoked OSN firing rate causing more release of glutamate in the glomerulus.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observed plasticity.

claim: Olfactory training could modify OSN turnover leading to higher number of axons innervating the same glomerulus.
source: Secondly, olfactory training could modify OSN turnover (Schwob et al., 1992) leading to higher number of axons innervating the same glomerulus (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A local network mechanism could alter OSN release through GABAB and dopamine D2 receptors.
source: Thirdly, a local network mechanism could alter OSN release. Since activation of GABAB (Aroniadou-Anderjaska et al., 2000; McGann et al., 2005) and dopamine D2 (Hsia et al., 1999; Ennis et al., 2001) receptors on OSN terminals can decrease glutamate release, inhibition of GABA and/or dopamine release would lead to the observed increase of input strength.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A direct increase in glutamate release mediated by neuromodulatory fibers may also account for the observed plasticity.
source: Finally, a direct increase in glutamate release mediated by neuromodulatory fibers may also account for the observed plasticity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the observed plasticity.

claim: Previous studies have shown how an animal can increase its breathing frequency when sampling an odor.
source: Previous studies have shown how an animal can increase its breathing frequency when sampling an odor (Verhagen et al., 2007; Carey et al., 2009; Wesson et al., 2009; Shusterman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The learning process can lead to a modulation of the respiration behavior in trained animals as compared to untrained animals.
source: The learning process can lead to a modulation of the respiration behavior in trained animals as compared to untrained animals.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge from previous research.

claim: Prolonged fast respiration (>4 Hz) reduces odor-evoked Ca2+ signals in OSNs.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that prolonged fast respiration (>4 Hz) reduces odor-evoked Ca2+ signals in OSNs (Verhagen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: No significant changes in the breathing frequency of mice were observed when monitored at the beginning and at the end of discrimination training.
source: However, we did not observe significant changes in the breathing frequency of mice when monitored at the beginning and at the end of discrimination training (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiration data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The breathing frequency was comparable to the one previously measured in naïve awake head-restrained animals (3.1 Hz).
source: The frequency was also comparable to the one previously measured in naïve awake head-restrained animals (3.1 Hz, Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: IOS amplitude does not vary with the animal's breathing frequency.
source: Likewise, IOS amplitude does not vary with the animal's breathing frequency (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The IOS potentiation mostly reflects neural changes induced by the learning process rather than respiration modulations.
source: Therefore, the IOS potentiation we report here mostly reflects neural changes induced by the learning process rather than respiration modulations.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the respiration data and IOS measurements.

claim: A similar potentiation of the odor-evoked glomeruli activity induced by fear learning has been reported in anesthetized animals where effects are presumably independent of respiration.
source: Along this line, a similar potentiation of the odor-evoked glomeruli activity induced by fear learning has been recently reported in anesthetized animals where effects are presumably independent of respiration (Kass et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The potential role played by breathing behavior is minor as a source of modulation of sensory input strength in olfactory associative learning tasks.
source: Altogether these data suggest that the potential role played by breathing behavior is minor as a source of modulation of sensory input strength in olfactory associative learning tasks.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the respiration and imaging data.

claim: The improved representations mediated by the training can account for discrimination accuracy and reaction time stability across a wide range of odorant dilutions.
source: What is the behavioral relevance of this plasticity? The improved representations mediated by the training can account for discrimination accuracy and reaction time stability across a wide range of odorant dilutions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral relevance of the findings.

claim: The observed increase in the sensitivity at higher dilutions of odorants tested should lower the odorant detection thresholds in mice.
source: The observed increase in the sensitivity at higher dilutions of odorants tested should lower the odorant detection thresholds in mice.
evidence: This is a predicted consequence of the observed plasticity.

claim: In human olfaction, trained wine tasters show lower detection thresholds and an increase in the perceived odorants intensity compare to healthy non-trained subjects.
source: Interestingly, in human olfaction, trained wine tasters show lower detection thresholds and an increase in the perceived odorants intensity compare to healthy non-trained subjects (Marino-Sanchez et al., 2010; Tempere et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in humans.

claim: The enhanced representation may be lasting for longer even with brief repetitive training and may account for the long lasting perception abilities seen in professional wine tasters.
source: Although the effect of the plasticity reported in our study lasted for 5 weeks, this enhanced representation may be lasting for longer even with brief repetitive training and may account for the long lasting perception abilities seen in professional wine tasters.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to human expertise.

claim: All experiments were performed on adult male C57BL/6J mice (11 weeks old at the beginning of the behavioral experiments).
source: All experiments were performed on adult male C57BL/6J mice (11 weeks old at the beginning of the behavioral experiments, Charles River France) in accordance with the Swiss Federal Act on Animal Protection and Swiss Animal Protection Ordinance, University of Geneva and the state of Geneva ethics committee (authorization 1007/3758/2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: Odorants used were iso-amyl acetate (IAA, ≥99% purity), ethyl butyrate (EB, ≥99%), 1,4-cineol (Cin, ≥85%), eugenol (Eu, ≥99%).
source: Odorants used were iso-amyl acetate (IAA, ≥99% purity), ethyl butyrate (EB, ≥99%), 1,4-cineol (Cin, ≥85%), eugenol (Eu, ≥99%).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimuli used.
